title: SPHEREx Seeing Through Dust
explanation:
What is blocking the center of the Milky Way? During its 13 billion years, our Milky Way has collected a lot of dust. In contrast to the skin cells, dirt, pollen, and other debris that make up the dust behind your couch, cosmic dust is hundreds of times smaller and made of tiny compounds of oxygen, carbon, and other elements released into space when a star dies. Today’s video shows infrared light from the Milky Way’s center gathered by NASA’s SPHEREx satellite. Each false color in the video corresponds to the infrared color associated with the wavelength shown in the top left. In the near-infrared, like 1.2 microns, light gets absorbed and scatters off of dust particles. SPHEREx then sees the Galactic Center almost entirely blocked by clouds of dust. In the mid-infrared, though, light is able to pierce through the dust and reach SPHEREx. This is similar to, but not exactly, why sunsets are red!

alt_text: The video captures the plane of the Milky Way where the plane runs through the horizontal center. There is a bright bulge at the center where a bunch of stars are clustered. Stars dot the sky above and below the plane. The video cycles through the different colors that SPHEREx captures. Some colors show that the starlight near the Milky Way center is mostly blocked by dust along the plane. Other colors are able to travel through the dust and reach SPHEREx, giving a clearer view of the brighter Milky Way center.
